parsed.main_gap: The proof never excludes negative values of g, so the asserted dichotomy for its range does not follow. This is readily repaired by iterating (4) until positivity of f is contradicted.

errors.description: At most one positive value does not imply that every value is 0 or c; negative values have not been ruled out. If g(x)=a<0, iterating (4) gives g(x+na)=a until the next point is nonpositive, contradicting f(t)=t+a>0.
errors.quote:
Consequently, either

* (i) $g\equiv 0$ (constant), which gives $f(x)=x$, a solution; or  
* (ii) there is $c>0$ such that $V \subseteq \{0, c\}$ with both values attainable.

errors.description: The dichotomy also omits the already-constant case V={c} with c>0. That case should be concluded immediately before treating the mixed range {0,c}.
errors.quote:
or  
* (ii) there is $c>0$ such that $V \subseteq \{0, c\}$ with both values attainable.

errors.description: There is a harmless expansion typo: for x in S_0 and y in S_c, A(x,y) contains 4cy, not 4cx. This term is unused because A is automatically positive.

parsed.notes: The main argument is strong and the answer and verification are correct. The missing nonnegativity lemma and omitted constant-positive branch are short, straightforward repairs, so the solution is essentially complete.
